html:
This dua — Allāhumma anta rabbī, lā ilāha illā anta… — is called by the Prophet ﷺ himself Sayyid al-Istighfār, "the master of seeking forgiveness." The naming is not honorific decoration; it is a classification. In the ḥadīth as recorded by al-Bukhārī (no. 6306) on the authority of Shaddād b. Aws, the Prophet ﷺ did not merely teach a dua — he ranked it. Sayyid in classical Arabic means "chief," "master," "the one above whom there is nothing of its kind." Ibn Ḥajar al-ʿAsqalānī, in his commentary Fatḥ al-Bārī, explains that the Prophet ﷺ used this term because the dua gathers in a single formula every component of a complete turning to Allah: creedal affirmation, servanthood, covenant, acknowledgment of divine favor, acknowledgment of sin, and petition for forgiveness grounded in the exclusive attribute of the Forgiver. No other short istighfār formula carries all six at once.

The dua opens with Allāhumma anta rabbī, lā ilāha illā ant — "O Allah, You are my Lord; there is no god but You." This is not a preamble. It is the tawḥīd foundation on which the entire petition rests. Ibn al-Qayyim, in Madārij al-Sālikīn, points out that the servant who seeks forgiveness without first affirming the lordship and uniqueness of the One being asked has, in a sense, come to a stranger with a request. The dua anchors the asker in the correct relationship before the asking begins. Al-Nawawī, in al-Adhkār, notes that this ordering — rabbī then lā ilāha illā ant — mirrors the shahādah: lordship (rubūbiyyah) acknowledged first, then godhood (ulūhiyyah). The servant is not inventing a theological entry point; he is reciting, in miniature, the covenant he already affirmed when he embraced Islam.

Then: khalaqtanī wa anā ʿabduk — "You created me and I am Your servant." Two statements, cause and consequence. Al-Ṭabarī, commenting on the parallel verse Qur'an 51:56 (wa mā khalaqtu l-jinna wa l-insa illā li-yaʿbudūn, "I did not create jinn and humans except to worship Me"), establishes the classical principle: creation itself obligates servanthood. The one who created has the exclusive right to be served; the one who was created has no identity apart from being a servant. The dua compresses that principle into five words. Note what the servant does not say: he does not say "I try to be Your servant" or "I hope I am Your servant." He states it as a fact of ontology — wa anā ʿabduk, "and I am Your servant," present-tense, unqualified. In the fiqh of istighfār, this matters: the one asking for forgiveness is first stating his standing. He is not a stranger petitioning a king; he is a servant returning to his Master.

Next comes the covenant clause: wa anā ʿalā ʿahdika wa waʿdika mastaṭaʿt — "and I keep Your covenant and promise as best I can." This is where the dua becomes psychologically honest in a way most short istighfār formulas are not. The servant does not claim to keep the covenant perfectly. He adds mastaṭaʿt — "to the extent of my capacity." Al-Qurṭubī in his al-Jāmiʿ li-Aḥkām al-Qurʾān, discussing the general principle fa-ttaqū Allāha mā-staṭaʿtum (Qur'an 64:16, "fear Allah to the extent of your capacity"), notes that Islamic law and prophetic adhkār consistently qualify obedience by capacity, never demanding what the servant cannot deliver. The dua embeds this directly: the servant affirms his intention to keep the covenant while admitting his reach is limited. Ibn Ḥajar comments that this clause is precisely why the dua is called sayyid: it refuses both overclaiming and despair. The servant neither pretends to perfection nor abandons the covenant because he cannot perfect it.

The ʿahd ("covenant") and waʿd ("promise") the dua references are debated by classical commentators. Ibn al-Qayyim, in al-Wābil al-Ṣayyib, holds that the ʿahd is the covenant Allah took from all human souls in pre-eternity (Qur'an 7:172 — alastu bi-rabbikum qālū balā), while the waʿd is the servant's own standing commitment to obey, renewed every time he enters prayer. Others, including al-Nawawī, read both terms as referring broadly to the obligations Islam places on the believer. Either reading produces the same practical reality: the servant is saying, "I am bound by what I accepted, and I am honoring it as far as I am able."

Then the dua pivots inward: aʿūdhu bika min sharri mā ṣanaʿt — "I seek refuge in You from the evil of what I have done." This is the first explicit acknowledgment of sin, and it is phrased with striking precision. The servant does not say "forgive the evil I have done" (that comes later). He says "I seek refuge from the evil of what I have done" — from, not of. Ibn Ḥajar notes that sin produces two kinds of harm: the sin itself, and the consequences that trail the sin — distance from Allah, hardness of heart, exposure to further sin, worldly loss, and loss in the Hereafter. The servant is seeking refuge from the aftermath. This is a mature theology of repentance: he is not only asking for the record to be cleared; he is asking to be shielded from the gravitational pull sin exerts even after it has been committed.

What follows is one of the most spiritually dense phrases in all of Islamic adhkār: abūʾu laka bi-niʿmatika ʿalayya, wa abūʾu bi-dhanbī — "I acknowledge Your favor upon me, and I acknowledge my sin." The verb abūʾu is the hinge. Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī, in al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, defines bāʾa as "to return to a settled place and remain there." The servant is not merely admitting the favor and the sin; he is settling into the acknowledgment. He is taking up residence in the awareness of both — the mercy he has received and the wrong he has done — and refusing to move off either. Ibn al-Qayyim writes in Madārij al-Sālikīn that this double acknowledgment is the hallmark of the ʿabd who is neither self-congratulatory nor crushed: he holds both niʿmah and dhanb in his hands at once and brings them both to his Lord.

The order matters. The dua places niʿmah before dhanb. Al-Qurṭubī comments on this ordering: a servant who acknowledges his sin without first acknowledging the favor risks a repentance tinged with despair, as if the sin outweighs everything. A servant who begins with niʿmah — "Your favor upon me" — enters the act of istighfār from gratitude rather than from the shame alone. The sin is admitted fully, but it is admitted against the backdrop of mercy. This is the Qur'anic register: innahu ghafūrun shakūr — Allah is both the Forgiver and the One who repays gratitude (Qur'an 35:30). The dua trains the servant to approach forgiveness in Allah's own tone.

The closing clause — faghfir lī, fa innahu lā yaghfirudh-dhunūba illā ant, "so forgive me, for none forgives sins but You" — is theologically careful. The servant does not say "forgive me because I have repented" or "forgive me because I have acknowledged." He says "forgive me, because none forgives sins but You." Ibn Kathīr, commenting on Qur'an 3:135 (wa man yaghfirudh-dhunūba illā-llāh, "and who forgives sins except Allah?"), explains that this is the final tawḥīd move of the dua: the servant stakes his hope on an exclusive divine attribute. There is no backup plan. If Allah does not forgive, no one will. This is why the dua carries weight — it comes to Allah as the only address at which the request can be filed, and it says so explicitly.

The ḥadīth concludes with the Prophet's ﷺ extraordinary promise: "Whoever says it during the day with firm faith in it and dies that same day before evening, he is among the people of Paradise; and whoever says it at night with firm faith in it and dies before morning, he is among the people of Paradise." This is the single most explicit guarantee attached to any short istighfār formula in the ṣaḥīḥ corpus. But — and this is where al-Nawawī and Ibn Ḥajar both halt the hasty reader — the promise is conditioned on mūqinan bihā, "with firm faith in it." Not reciting it. Not mumbling it. Faith in it. The classical commentators spend considerable space on what yaqīn means here. Ibn Ḥajar: it is "believing in its meaning, intending its content, and living (as far as one is able) by what one is saying." Al-Nawawī: it is "the opposite of saying it with the tongue while the heart is somewhere else." The dua is not a password. It is a claim the servant is making about his standing before Allah, and the servant has to actually mean the claim.

This is why the fiqh of sayyid al-istighfār is both expansive and demanding. Ibn Taymiyyah, in Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā, categorizes it as part of the morning and evening adhkār, to be said twice a day as standard practice. Ibn al-Qayyim, in Zād al-Maʿād, places it among the "daily protection" formulas — spiritual armor that a believer wears into the day and takes off at night. But both scholars note the same caveat: the formula does its work when it is meant, not when it is merely recited. A believer who says it absentmindedly at the end of his morning routine while thinking about his inbox has said the words but has not entered the dua. A believer who stops, situates himself before Allah, and recites it with awareness of each clause has entered one of the most highly ranked spiritual acts available in the daily life of a Muslim.

Where to say it, and how to think about the promise

Classical practice places this dua in three canonical contexts. First, in the morning adhkār (after Fajr), once. Second, in the evening adhkār (after ʿAṣr or Maghrib), once. These two placements are directly tied to the Prophetic promise — if one dies during the day having said it in the morning with yaqīn, or during the night having said it in the evening, the ḥadīth gives Paradise as the result. Third, as a general istighfār formula whenever the servant feels the need for a more complete and theologically full turning to Allah than the shorter astaghfirullāh affords.

The ḥadīth's promise should not be read as a transactional guarantee that bypasses the usual requirements of repentance. Al-Nawawī explicitly addresses this: the ḥadīth does not say that someone can persist in major sin, recite the dua at the end of the day with yaqīn, die, and enter Paradise regardless. The yaqīn clause includes intending the dua's content, and the dua's content includes abūʾu bi-dhanbī ("I acknowledge my sin") and faghfir lī ("forgive me") — which is itself a repentance. A servant who says this dua with full awareness of what he is saying has, in that moment, engaged in tawbah. The promise is for the one whose last act in the day was a genuine turning. It is extraordinary, but it is not a loophole.

Equally, the promise should not be read as creating anxiety — "I only said it mechanically; am I lost?" The Prophet ﷺ taught the dua for people's benefit, not to burden them. Ibn Ḥajar notes that even saying it without the full depth of yaqīn is still a form of istighfār that carries ordinary reward; the ḥadīth's specific guarantee of Paradise-upon-same-day-death is the upper bound of the dua's effect, not its only effect. A believer who says it daily with the intention of yaqīn, and whose attention wavers some mornings as human attention does, has not lost the dua. He has engaged in the ordinary practice of a believer, and Allah, who is ghafūr raḥīm, deals with servants according to His vastness, not according to the servant's best moment.

There is one practical pitfall worth naming. The dua's power is tied to its being said in full and understood. Shortening it (dropping the abūʾu clauses, or omitting the final fa innahu lā yaghfirudh-dhunūba illā ant) collapses the dua's theological architecture and places the reciter outside the specific ḥadīth. The shorter istighfār formulas (e.g. Rabbighfir lī wa tub ʿalayya) are their own ṣaḥīḥ practice with their own merits — but they are not this dua, and the Bukhārī 6306 promise is attached to this wording. Memorize the full text. Recite it as given. Let its length be the thing that stops you in the morning and makes you actually mean it, rather than something to be rushed through.

sources.label: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6306 — Kitāb al-Daʿawāt, Bāb Afḍal al-Istighfār
sources.note: primary textual basis; Shaddād b. Aws narration; the Prophet ﷺ names this dua Sayyid al-Istighfār and promises Paradise to the one who dies that day/night having said it with yaqīn

sources.label: Ibn Ḥajar al-ʿAsqalānī — Fatḥ al-Bārī bi-Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī
sources.note: on no. 6306; why this dua is called sayyid (it gathers tawḥīd, servanthood, covenant, niʿmah, dhanb, and petition in one formula); yaqīn condition unpacked as 'believing the meaning + intending the content + living by it as far as one is able'

sources.label: al-Nawawī — al-Adhkār + Riyāḍ al-Ṣāliḥīn (Kitāb al-Istighfār)
sources.note: ordering of rabbī and lā ilāha illā anta mirrors the shahādah; yaqīn is the opposite of tongue-moving while the heart is absent; promise is not a loophole bypassing ordinary tawbah

sources.label: Ibn al-Qayyim — Madārij al-Sālikīn + al-Wābil al-Ṣayyib + Zād al-Maʿād
sources.note: the servant settles (bāʾa) into both niʿmah and dhanb at once as the hallmark of mature servanthood; ʿahd as the pre-eternal covenant of Qur'an 7:172; placement in daily morning/evening adhkār as spiritual armor

sources.label: al-Qurṭubī — al-Jāmiʿ li-Aḥkām al-Qurʾān
sources.note: on Qur'an 64:16 (fa-ttaqū Allāha mā-staṭaʿtum); the mastaṭaʿt qualifier anchors Islamic obligation to capacity; ordering niʿmah before dhanb prevents repentance tinged with despair

sources.label: al-Ṭabarī — Jāmiʿ al-Bayān (on Qur'an 51:56)
sources.note: creation obligates servanthood as a matter of ontology, not aspiration; wa anā ʿabduk is stated as fact, not hope

sources.label: Ibn Kathīr — Tafsīr al-Qurʾān al-ʿAẓīm (on Qur'an 3:135)
sources.note: wa man yaghfirudh-dhunūba illā-llāh — the dua's closing clause stakes hope on an exclusive divine attribute; no backup address for forgiveness

sources.label: Ibn Taymiyyah — Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā; al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān
sources.note: Ibn Taymiyyah: classification among the standard morning/evening adhkār (twice daily); al-Rāghib: the verb bāʾa means 'to return to a settled place and remain there' — the servant takes up residence in dual acknowledgment
